<html>

  <body>
    <p style="margin-top: 0px">
      Yes &#8212; it uses only Go's standard library: <code>testing</code> 
      (built&#8209;in test runner) plus <code>net/http/httptest</code> (stdlib 
      HTTP test helpers). No third&#8209;party assertion framework like testify.
    </p>
    <h2>
      What it tests
    </h2>
    <p>
      It exercises the router from <a href="#">server.go</a> &#8212; <code>newRouter</code>, 
      <code>helloWorldPath</code>, <code>helloWorldHandler</code> &#8212; without 
      starting a real network server.
    </p>
    <h3>
      <code>TestRouter</code>
    </h3>
    <p>
      A <strong>table&#8209;driven test</strong> (the idiomatic Go pattern): a 
      slice of anonymous structs describes each case (<code>method</code>, <code>path</code>, 
      <code>wantStatus</code>, <code>wantBody</code>), and <code>t.Run(tc.name, 
      ...)</code> creates a named subtest per case so failures report which 
      one broke.
    </p>
    <p>
      Per case:
    </p>
    <ul>
      <li>
        <code>httptest.NewRequest(method, path, nil)</code> builds an 
        in&#8209;memory <code>*http.Request</code>.
      </li>
      <li>
        <code>httptest.NewRecorder()</code> is a fake <code>http.ResponseWriter</code> 
        that captures status, headers, body.
      </li>
      <li>
        <code>router.ServeHTTP(rec, req)</code> calls the handler directly &#8212; 
        no listening socket, no ports, fast and deterministic.
      </li>
      <li>
        Assertions are plain <code>if</code> + <code>t.Fatalf</code>, which is 
        how the stdlib style works (no assert library).
      </li>
    </ul>
    <p>
      The cases document the Go 1.22+ <code>ServeMux</code> behavior from the <code>&quot;GET 
      &quot;+path</code> pattern:
    </p>
    <table>
      <tr>
        <th>
          Case
        </th>
        <th>
          Expected
        </th>
        <th>
          Why
        </th>
      </tr>
      <tr>
        <td>
          GET <code>/api/v1/hello-world</code>
        </td>
        <td>
          200 + <code>Hello, World!</code>
        </td>
        <td>
          registered route
        </td>
      </tr>
      <tr>
        <td>
          GET <code>/nope</code>
        </td>
        <td>
          404
        </td>
        <td>
          no pattern matches
        </td>
      </tr>
      <tr>
        <td>
          HEAD on the path
        </td>
        <td>
          200
        </td>
        <td>
          mux matches HEAD via the GET pattern
        </td>
      </tr>
      <tr>
        <td>
          POST / DELETE
        </td>
        <td>
          405
        </td>
        <td>
          mux rejects other verbs automatically
        </td>
      </tr>
    </table>
    <p>
      Note <code>wantBody</code> is only checked when non&#8209;empty, and it's 
      compared after <code>strings.TrimSpace</code>.
    </p>
    <h3>
      <code>TestMethodNotAllowedSetsAllowHeader</code>
    </h3>
    <p>
      Asserts that a POST gets 405 <strong>and</strong> that the mux sets the <code>Allow</code> 
      response header containing <code>GET</code> &#8212; proving the 405/Allow 
      logic comes from the standard mux, not from hand&#8209;written validation in <code>helloWorldHandler</code>.
    </p>
    <h2>
      Running it
    </h2>
    <pre data-copilot-type="code-block" data-copilot-offset="1798,1832" data-copilot-content-offset="1812,1829" data-copilot-code-block-index="0" data-copilot-code-language="powershell"><code>go test ./... -v</code></pre>
  </body>
</html>

#### Answer **
<html>
  <head>

  <body>
    <p style="margin-top: 0px">
      There's no assertion library &#8212; the &quot;assertions&quot; are hand&#8209;written <code>if</code> 
      checks followed by <code>t.Fatalf</code>, which marks the test failed 
      and stops that subtest immediately.
    </p>
    <p>
      In <a href="#">server_test.go</a>:
    </p>
    <p>
      <strong>Status code assertion</strong> (lines 61&#8209;63, inside the <code>t.Run</code> 
      subtest):
    </p>
    <pre data-copilot-type="code-block" data-copilot-offset="328,432" data-copilot-content-offset="334,429" data-copilot-code-block-index="0" data-copilot-code-language="go"><code>if rec.Code != tc.wantStatus {
    t.Fatalf(&quot;status = %d, want %d&quot;, rec.Code, tc.wantStatus)
}</code></pre>
    <p>
      <strong>Body assertion</strong> (lines 65&#8209;69) &#8212; only runs when the case 
      specifies an expected body:
    </p>
    <pre data-copilot-type="code-block" data-copilot-offset="521,691" data-copilot-content-offset="527,688" data-copilot-code-block-index="1" data-copilot-code-language="go"><code>if tc.wantBody != &quot;&quot; {
    if got := strings.TrimSpace(rec.Body.String()); got != tc.wantBody {
        t.Fatalf(&quot;body = %q, want %q&quot;, got, tc.wantBody)
    }
}</code></pre>
    <p>
      <strong>In <code>TestMethodNotAllowedSetsAllowHeader</code></strong> 
      (lines 80&#8209;86):
    </p>
    <pre data-copilot-type="code-block" data-copilot-offset="753,1037" data-copilot-content-offset="759,1034" data-copilot-code-block-index="2" data-copilot-code-language="go"><code>if rec.Code != http.StatusMethodNotAllowed {
    t.Fatalf(&quot;status = %d, want %d&quot;, rec.Code, http.StatusMethodNotAllowed)
}

if got := rec.Header().Get(&quot;Allow&quot;); !strings.Contains(got, http.MethodGet) {
t.Fatalf(&quot;Allow = %q, want it to contain %q&quot;, got, http.MethodGet)
}</code></pre>
<p>
The values being asserted on come from the <code>httptest.ResponseRecorder</code>
(<code>rec</code>): <code>rec.Code</code>, <code>rec.Body</code>, <code>rec.Header()</code>.
<code>t.Fatalf</code> = fail + <code>runtime.Goexit()</code>; use <code>t.Errorf</code>
instead if you want the remaining checks in the same subtest to still
run.
</p>
  </body>
</html>

#### Author

#### Prompt
<html>
  <head>

  </head>
  <body>
    <p style="margin-top: 0px">
      Is this really the go way of making unit tests?
    </p>
  </body>
</html>


#### Answer **
<html>
  <head>

  </head>
  <body>
    <p style="margin-top: 0px">
      Yes &#8212; this is essentially textbook idiomatic Go. The conventions it 
      follows are the same ones used inside the Go standard library itself:
    </p>
    <ol>
      <li>
        <strong>Stdlib <code>testing</code> only.</strong> Go deliberately 
        ships a minimal test framework with no assertions, no <code>setUp</code>/<code>tearDown</code>, 
        no annotations. The <a href="https://go.dev/wiki/TestComments">official 
        FAQ/CodeReviewComments</a> explicitly discourage assertion DSLs 
        because failure messages should say <em>what</em> was wrong, not just 
        &quot;assertion failed&quot;.
      </li>
      <li>
        <strong>Table&#8209;driven subtests.</strong> <code>[]struct{...}</code> 
        + <code>t.Run(name, ...)</code> is the single most common test pattern 
        in Go. It lets you run one case with <code>go test -run 
        'TestRouter/wrong_method'</code>.
      </li>
      <li>
        <strong><code>got</code>/<code>want</code> message style.</strong> <code>t.Fatalf(&quot;status 
        = %d, want %d&quot;, ...)</code> matches the stdlib's standard 
        phrasing.
      </li>
      <li>
        <strong><code>httptest</code> instead of a real server.</strong> 
        Calling <code>handler.ServeHTTP(rec, req)</code> directly is the 
        recommended way to test HTTP handlers &#8212; no ports, no flakiness.
      </li>
    </ol>
    <h3>
      Where reasonable Go devs differ
    </h3>
    <ul>
      <li>
        <strong>testify.</strong> Very widely used in industry (<code>assert.Equal(t, 
        want, got)</code>). Legit choice, but it's a third&#8209;party dependency 
        and the core team's style guides still prefer plain <code>if</code>. 
        For a small API like this, plain <code>if</code> is fine.
      </li>
      <li>
        <strong><code>t.Parallel()</code>.</strong> Since these subtests are 
        independent and stateless, you could add <code>t.Parallel()</code> at 
        the top of each <code>t.Run</code> closure. (Note: with Go 1.22+ 
        loop&#8209;variable semantics you no longer need the <code>tc := tc</code> 
        copy.)
      </li>
      <li>
        <strong><code>t.Errorf</code> vs <code>t.Fatalf</code>.</strong> Using <code>Fatal</code> 
        for the status check is right here &#8212; if the status is wrong, checking 
        the body is noise. That's the correct judgement call.
      </li>
      <li>
        <strong>Naming.</strong> Some prefer <code>cases</code> over <code>tests</code>, 
        and putting <code>router := newRouter()</code> inside the subtest for 
        isolation. Cosmetic.
      </li>
    </ul>
    <p>
      One small critique: the <code>if tc.wantBody != &quot;&quot;</code> 
      guard means &quot;expect an empty body&quot; can't be expressed. If you ever need 
      that, a <code>*string</code> or a separate <code>checkBody bool</code> 
      field would be needed. Minor, and common in real code.
    </p>
    <p>
      Verdict: no changes needed &#8212; this is how a Go reviewer would want it 
      written.
    </p>
  </body>
</html>
